newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: US, EU worried over SKorean anti-import campaign.
newsitem.headline: US, EU worried over SKorean anti-import campaign.

text.p: Major trading blocs, including the United States and European Union, sought reassurances from South Korea on Tuesday that it was not encouraging "anti-import" campaigns, trade diplomats said.
Dr. Han Duck-Soo, deputy minister for trade, responded that his government would not resort to or encourage such campaigns or any import discriminating policies, they added.

The exchange took place during a closed-door examination of a report by the World Trade Organisation (WTO) which hailed South Korea, the world's 12th largest trading nation, as "one of the world's most dynamic economies".

The global watchdog, in a report on South Korea's trade policies, urged Seoul to step up the pace of opening up to the outside world. It also suggested that the government was sometimes ready to implement liberalisation in key areas of the economy only in response to outside pressures.
Han, aided by South Korean trade ambassador Joun Yung Sun, formerly deputy minister of economic affairs at the foreign ministry, led a 20-strong team from Seoul for the two-day talks.

Anne Anderson, Ireland's ambassador who chairs the WTO's Trade Policy Review Body, said that South Korea's trading partners had praised its rapid economic growth and continued trade liberalisation since the last review in 1992.

"Members noted, however, the export promotion efforts adopted in response to the recent rise in the current account deficit, and sought confirmation that no public or private 'anti-import' campaigns or other restrictive policies would be undertaken," she said in a written summary statement.
"Four or five delegations raised this issue. There was concern that the campaign was taking hold, developing popular support," Anderson later told a news briefing.
The U.S. and EU trade delegations were among those who took the floor to express concern, she said in response to a query.
Anderson, referring to Han, wrote: "He confirmed that the (South) Korean government would not resort to or encourage 'anti-import' campaigns or import discriminating rules."

South Korea's ambassador Sun, in an opening speech to the meeting, said that his country's current account had deteriorated. By the end of August, its current account deficit had surged to a "record high level" of more than $15 billion.
"Despite these recent trends, the (South) Korean government has steadfastly maintained its commitment to trade liberalisation," Sun said.
Delegations welcomed South Korea's tariff cuts since the Uruguay Round, but questioned the lack of bound tariffs for fishery products and various strategic industrial goods.
Major partners expressed concern over the slow pace of Seoul's implementation of non-tariff reform, including customs clearance procedures, import licensing and inspection procedure.
The WTO, noting South Korean growth exceeded nine per cent in 1995, said the stimulus came from buoyant exports in the wake of the appreciating Japanese yen and strong domestic investment.

"Strong economic growth, deregulation, trade liberalisation and an easing of foreign investment restrictions are helping (South) Korea not only to become more competitive but also take a more forceful approach to domestic reform," the report said.

South Korea was in the end phase of a five-year plan (1993-97) to cut state control, abolish unnecessary regulations and restrictions, increase transparency of trade-related policies, and align domestic law with international regulations.

However, WTO's 147-page report said that reforms in agriculture -- where heavy protection of the key rice sector has brought South Korea frequent criticism from many trading partners -- had been driven mainly by external requirements "rather than efficiency considerations or consumer welfare."
